lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What does it take to turn a few numbers in a matrix into a cube spinning on your screen? Antoine's Rust project Dimension answers that, one layer at a time.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, so where does a project like that start?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: With the math library, called mathlib. It stores matrices in dense form and in sparse formats, and gives you vectors, views and submatrices. On top of that it offers classic numerical tools: LU, Cholesky and SVD decompositions, root finding and numerical integration.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like a linear algebra textbook.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A bit, yes, and that's the point. The renderer reuses those same pieces on the CPU for transforms and camera math. So the math isn't a separate experiment, it feeds the drawing.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does the drawing part work?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a flow: geometry goes into CPU transforms, then into a scene with cameras, then into a renderer built on wgpu. That renderer can show the result in a native window or in a web canvas through WebAssembly.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A world of entities, each with a transform, plus cameras and render targets. The scene is a tree of parents and children. Think of a hand holding a cup: move the hand, and the cup moves with it, because the cup's position is described relative to the hand.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's neat. And keeping native and web separate?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Platform code lives in its own layer, apart from the scene and the numerical code, so both targets share the same building blocks. There's also optional serialization through the serde feature, and optional GPU functionality behind a feature flag.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is it only math and rendering?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The workspace is wider. Antoine's manifest lists crates for geometry, collision, kinematics, physics, networking, parsing and neural work next to mathlib. He reads the manifest and module entry points to see how it all fits together.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is a clean path from matrices to pixels.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes: storage, transforms, scene, renderer. And you don't have to take it on faith: the page runs the demos right in your browser. Press start and you get the render demo, the geometry meshes, the math library and the embeddings, all compiled to WebAssembly. The full write-up has the architecture diagram and links to each source file.
